title: Rotate Array
description: Brute force to optimized: one step at a time versus direct placement versus the in place three reversal trick.

blocks.text: 1. Problem Statement
Problem Summary: Given an array nums and an integer k, rotate the array to the right by k steps, in place, so the last k elements wrap around to the front while everything else shifts right.

blocks.text: 3. Understand the Problem
Given an array nums and an integer k, rotate the array to the right by k steps, in place, so the last k elements wrap around to the front while everything else shifts right.

blocks.title: Analogy: A Rotating Display Case
blocks.text: Like a rotating display case in a shop window: pushing it a few steps moves everything along in the same direction, and whatever falls off the visible end simply reappears at the start.

blocks.caption: Every element shifts right by k positions, wrapping around at the end

blocks.text: Edge case: k equals the array length
When k is a multiple of the array's length, every element rotates all the way back to its own original position, so the array is unchanged.
5. How Should We Think?
It helps to ask what a right rotation by k actually does to each individual index, rather than thinking of it only as a whole array operation.

blocks.title: How Should We Think?
blocks.text:
Observation 1: The most literal reading, "shift everything right by one, k times", is correct but repeats almost identical work on every single step, since nearly the whole array moves again and again.

Observation 2: Every element at index i has one specific final destination, index (i plus k) modulo n, so computing that destination directly and placing the value there once removes the repeated shifting entirely.

Observation 3: But a fresh result array still costs O(n) extra space. Reverse-a-string already showed that reversing a sequence in place needs only a two pointer swap from both ends, no extra storage at all.

Observation 4: A right rotation by k is exactly equivalent to three such in place reversals in sequence, reverse everything, then reverse the first k elements, then reverse the remaining n minus k elements, turning a rotation into pure reversal with zero extra array.

Recognizing rotation as "three reversals in disguise" is what turns an O(n) extra space solution into a true O(1) extra space one, by reusing the same in place reversal idea from simpler string and array problems.
6. Brute Force Solution
Rotate the entire array one step at a time, repeating k times (after first reducing k modulo the array length, since a full rotation of length n changes nothing).
Step by step algorithm

items: Reduce k modulo the array length, since rotating by the full length changes nothing.
Repeat k times: take the last element off the array and reinsert it at the front.

codes.python:
def rotate(nums, k):
    n = len(nums)
    k %= n                                                  # rotating by a full length changes nothing
    for _ in range(k):                                        # repeat one single step rotation k times
        last = nums.pop()
        nums.insert(0, last)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    nums = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7]
    rotate(nums, 3)
    print(nums)

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: k is reduced modulo n first, since any multiple of a full rotation leaves the array exactly as it started.
Each single step rotation shifts every element right by exactly one position, moving the freed last element to the front.
Repeating this single step k times reaches the correct final rotation, but redoes nearly the same full array shift on every repetition.

blocks.text: 7. Analyze the Brute Force
Each single step rotation correctly moves every element one position to the right, so repeating it k times produces the correct final rotation.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n times k), since every one of the k single step rotations shifts all n elements.
Space: O(1) extra, the array is shifted in place.
Limitation: shifting the whole array by one position, k separate times, redoes almost all of the same work over and over instead of placing every element directly at its final position in one pass.
8. Optimize the Solution

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text:
Why the brute force works but is wasteful: repeating a full array shift k separate times touches almost every element k times over, instead of once.

What direct placement fixes: every element at index i belongs at exactly index (i plus k) modulo n in the final array, so writing it there directly, in a single pass into a fresh array, needs each element touched only once.

Can the extra array be avoided: yes, since a right rotation by k is mathematically identical to reversing the whole array, then reversing its first k elements, then reversing its remaining elements.

The core idea: direct placement removes the repeated shifting first, and the three reversal trick then removes the extra array on top of that, using the same in place two pointer swap idea from simpler reversal problems.

Every element at index i belongs at index (i plus k) modulo n in the rotated array. Instead of shifting step by step, build a new array and place every value directly at its final computed position in a single pass, then copy that new array back over the original.
9. Optimized Solution
Compute each element's final position directly and place it there in one pass.
Dry run for nums = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7], k = 3

blocks.caption: Optimized: place every value directly at its final rotated position

blocks.text: Why This Works

This works because rotating right by k is defined as sending every value at index i to index (i plus k) modulo n, so computing that formula once per element and writing directly into a fresh array reproduces the exact same final arrangement as repeated shifting, without any repeated work.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n), a single pass to place every element and one to copy back.
Space: O(n), for the separate result array.
10. Further Optimization: Three Reversals, In Place

Rotating to the right by k is equivalent to reversing the whole array, then reversing just the first k elements, and finally reversing the remaining n minus k elements. This produces the exact same result using no extra array at all, only in place reversals.
Dry run for nums = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7], k = 3

blocks.content: {"headers":["Step","Array state"],"rows":[["Reverse the whole array","[7, 6, 5, 4, 3, 2, 1]"],["Reverse the first k = 3 elements","[5, 6, 7, 4, 3, 2, 1]"],["Reverse the remaining n minus k = 4 elements","[5, 6, 7, 1, 2, 3, 4]"]]}

blocks.caption: Further optimization: three in place reversals produce the rotation with no extra array

codes.python:
def rotate(nums, k):
    n = len(nums)
    k %= n

    def reverse(left, right):
        while left < right:
            nums[left], nums[right] = nums[right], nums[left]
            left += 1
            right -= 1

    reverse(0, n - 1)                                       # reverse the whole array
    reverse(0, k - 1)                                        # reverse the first k elements
    reverse(k, n - 1)                                         # reverse the remaining elements


if __name__ == "__main__":
    nums = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7]
    rotate(nums, 3)
    print(nums)

blocks.text: Code walkthrough

items: Reversing the entire array first flips every element's relative order, including sending the elements that should end up at the front to the very front, but backward.
Reversing just the first k elements of that flipped array un-reverses them back into their correct relative order, since they were only flipped by the first step.
Reversing the remaining n minus k elements does the same correction for the second segment, leaving the whole array in its final correctly rotated order using only in place swaps.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n), three reversals that together touch each element a constant number of times.
Space: O(1), everything happens in place with no extra array.

blocks.text: 12. Key Takeaways
The three reversal trick used in the further round is a general technique for in place rotation, and shows up again in string rotation and word reordering problems, not just this exact one.
Common Mistakes

items: Forgetting to reduce k modulo n first, which can cause far more rotation steps than necessary or index errors in the direct placement approach.
Reversing the wrong two segments, or reversing them in the wrong order, in the three reversal approach.

blocks.text: Edge Cases

blocks.content: {"headers":["Case","Expected Behavior"],"rows":[["k equal to 0, or a multiple of the array length","The array is left unchanged."],["A single element array","Trivially unaffected by any rotation."]]}

blocks.text: Interview Tips
Present the direct placement approach first since it is the most intuitive O(n) time, O(n) space solution, then offer the three reversal trick as the in place follow up.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text:
If the interviewer says "can you do this without extra space", think: the three reversal trick, reverse the whole array, then each of the two segments.
If the interviewer says "what if k is much larger than n", think: reduce k modulo n first, since a full rotation changes nothing.
If the interviewer says "why do three reversals equal one rotation", think: the first reversal flips everything, and the next two reversals correct each segment's internal order back to normal.
Interview Follow-up Questions

items: Why does reversing the whole array, then each of its two segments, reproduce a right rotation exactly?
How would you adapt this approach to rotate the array to the left instead of to the right?
What changes if k could be negative?
How would you rotate a singly linked list by k nodes instead of an array?
How would this approach change if the array were extremely large and stored across multiple machines?

blocks.text: Pattern Connections

items: Reverse a String, whose two pointer in place reversal is the exact building block reused three times here.
Product of Array Except Self, whose prefix and suffix passes show the same "precompute a direct formula instead of repeating work" instinct applied to a different operation.
Any array or string problem asking for an in place transformation with O(1) extra space, where decomposing the operation into a sequence of reversals or swaps is often the key insight.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: Brute force: O(n times k) time, O(1) space. Optimized: O(n) time, O(n) space. Further optimized (three reversals): O(n) time, O(1) space.
13. Final Summary

items: Pattern: index arithmetic for direct placement, further reduced to the three reversal trick for an in place rotation.

Core Idea: a right rotation by k sends every value at index i to index (i plus k) modulo n, and this exact rearrangement can also be produced with zero extra space by reversing the whole array and then each of its two segments.
Time: O(n times k) for the brute force, O(n) for both optimized versions.
Space: O(1) extra for the brute force, O(n) extra for direct placement, O(1) extra for the three reversal trick.
Most Important Observation: a rotation can be decomposed into a small, fixed sequence of in place reversals, removing the need for any extra array entirely.
Interview Difficulty: direct placement is easy to derive; proving why three reversals reproduce a rotation is what shows real algorithmic insight.
One line memory trick: reverse it all, then reverse each half back into place.
